title: Copilot Studio: share autonomous agents with end users (run-only)
summary: Hold: the data-policy command creates a policy but does not document the connector blocking the table promises. The data-policy path stops before selecting Block, and the spending-policy path omits the Resources scope choice. The roadmap, licensing prerequisites and preview behaviour are supported.

claims.claim: This roadmap item concerns Microsoft Copilot Studio.
claims.quote: "products": ["Microsoft Copilot Studio"]

claims.claim: The roadmap description says autonomous agents previously could only be used and managed by makers.
claims.quote: Previously, autonomous agents could only be used and managed by makers, limiting their reach to the people who needed them.

claims.claim: Run-only sharing is intended to let end users benefit without edit permissions or ownership.
claims.quote: Run-only sharing enables makers to securely share autonomous agents with end users, allowing users to benefit from agent-driven automation without requiring edit permissions or ownership.

claims.claim: A maker can share a published autonomous agent that has triggers.
claims.quote: You can share a published agent that has triggers with users who need to run the agent by using their own credentials.

claims.claim: Run-only recipients can be individual users or security groups.
claims.quote: Enter the user name, email addresses of individual users, or security groups you want to share the agent with. Ensure Can use appears beside the search bar.

claims.where: summary; What's changing; Why it matters; Risk assessment; rationale: risk
claims.claim: Recipients run the shared agent with their own credentials and connections.
claims.quote: Recipients can use the can use link to activate the agent for themselves, connect the agent with their own credentials, and manage their permitted trigger settings.

claims.claim: Before run-only sharing, triggers and tools must be configured for user authentication.
claims.quote: Before sharing, configure the agent's triggers and tools for user authentication.

claims.claim: Recipients activate a shared agent for themselves rather than sharing alone starting their runs.
claims.quote: Recipients can use the can use link to activate the agent for themselves, connect the agent with their own credentials, and manage their permitted trigger settings.

claims.claim: Learn documents run-only sharing as preview and its related experience as prerelease.
claims.quote:
# Add triggers to an agent (Microsoft Copilot) (preview)

[This article is prerelease documentation and is subject to change.]

claims.claim: The maker selects Agents > agent > Share > Can use to grant run-only access.
claims.quote:
Open the agent from the Agents page.
...
If you already shared the agent with users, change their permission to Can use.

claims.where: What's changing; Governance guidance: At rollout; controls[6].note
claims.claim: Makers must copy and send the Copy link to set up link to recipients.
claims.quote:
Select Copy sharing link, then Copy link to set up.
6. Send the link to the end users you shared the autonomous agent with.

claims.where: What's changing; Risk assessment: Change & support
claims.claim: Recipients receive no sharing notification.
claims.quote: Sharing visibility: Users don't receive a notification when a maker shares an agent with them.

claims.claim: The agent cannot run until the recipient connects every trigger, tool and workflow that requires their credentials.
claims.quote: An autonomous agent can't run until you connect every trigger, tool, and workflow that requires your credentials.

claims.claim: Makers use Editable by user to choose which trigger options recipients may change.
claims.quote: If you're sharing this agent with others to use, choose which options users can or can't configure themselves by turning on or off Editable by user for each option.

claims.claim: Recipients cannot change instructions, tools or other authoring settings.
claims.quote: You can't change the agent's instructions, tools, or other authoring settings.

claims.where: What's changing; Risk assessment: Autonomy & actions; Scope
claims.claim: Recipients cannot specify or modify tool parameters.
claims.quote: Users of a shared autonomous agent can't specify or modify tool parameters.

claims.where: What's changing; Risk assessment: Autonomy & actions
claims.claim: Tool calls are invoked and executed fully with AI, based on the maker's specifications.
claims.quote: Tool calls are invoked and executed fully with AI, based on the maker's specifications.

claims.claim: A workflow used as a tool by the shared autonomous agent accepts only end-user credentials.
claims.quote: If your agent calls a workflow as a tool, that workflow can only accept end user credentials for authentication. Workflows that use any maker-only credentials aren't supported for autonomous agents.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Security & identity; Governance guidance: At rollout
claims.claim: Maker updates prompt recipients to accept changes and can require new or updated connections on the management page.
claims.quote: Republish the agent after you change a trigger, its instructions, or its tools. Updating an agent prompts users to accept the new changes.

claims.claim: Users need to bookmark the management URL to check health, fix connections and consent to maker updates.
claims.quote: End users need to bookmark the agent management URL to check their agent's health, fix the agent, consent to maker updates to the agent, and other management tasks.

claims.claim: End-user-authenticated actions operate within the recipient's permissions.
claims.quote: No stored maker credentials are used at run time, aligning the agent's behavior with the end user's actual permissions.

claims.claim: The agent's instructions and tools determine what it does with trigger event data.
claims.quote: The trigger sends event details to the agent. Your agent's instructions and tools determine what the agent does with those details.

claims.where: Risk assessment: Autonomy & actions; rationale: risk
claims.claim: Autonomous runs can start from events without someone opening a chat or prompting the agent.
claims.quote: Autonomous agents run when an event occurs in a connected service. For example, an agent can respond when an item is created in SharePoint, an email arrives, or a scheduled time occurs.

claims.claim: Recipients can pause and resume triggers with the Enabled toggle.
claims.quote: To pause a trigger without removing its configuration, turn the Enabled toggle off. Turn it on again when you want the trigger to run.

claims.claim: The management page's Activity tab shows recent runs and failures.
claims.quote: Use the Activity tab to review recent runs and identify failed runs.

claims.where: licensing.notes; Cost and licensing; controls[6].note; rationale: cost
claims.claim: The sharing prerequisites require recipients to have a Microsoft Copilot Studio per-user licence.
claims.quote: Users you share with have a Microsoft Copilot Studio per-user license.

claims.claim: The sharing article says users without a licence can sign up for a trial.
claims.quote: Users who don't have a license can sign up for a trial.

claims.where: Cost and licensing; Governance guidance: At rollout

claims.quote: Agents you want to share are published to Teams + Microsoft 365, with Make agent available in Microsoft Copilot turned on.

claims.claim: The sharing prerequisites specify Authenticate with Microsoft.
claims.quote: User authentication for the agent is configured to Authenticate with Microsoft.

claims.where: summary; licensing.notes; Cost and licensing; rationale: cost
claims.claim: Each end user's autonomous usage is totalled and billed through the environment hosting the agent.
claims.quote: Each end user's autonomous agent usage is totaled and billed through the underlying environment where the agent is hosted.

claims.claim: Usage is measured and billed in Copilot Credits.
claims.quote: Usage is billed based on consumption and measured in Copilot Credits.

claims.claim: Microsoft Copilot harness credits cover LLM tokens, tools and the harness itself.
claims.quote: For experiences powered by the Microsoft Copilot harness, Copilot Credits are charged for large language model (LLM) tokens, tools (including knowledge and MCPs), and the harness itself.

claims.claim: Power Platform administrators can manage Copilot Credits and allocate them to environments in the Power Platform admin center.
claims.quote: Copilot Credits are managed through the Power Platform admin center. Administrators can allocate credits to environments and monitor usage to ensure that sufficient credits are available.

claims.claim: A Microsoft 365 resource-based spending policy can cover particular agents or environments.
claims.quote: Manage Copilot Studio spending in the Microsoft 365 admin center by creating policies for environments or individual agents.

claims.where: Cost and licensing; Governance guidance: Before rollout
claims.claim: Resource-based spending policies offer a monthly limit and an optional per-agent limit.
claims.quote: Choose No limit or set a monthly spending limit for the policy. You can also set a per-agent limit so that no single agent covered by the policy uses more than the amount you specify.

claims.where: Cost and licensing; controls[5].note; Governance controls
claims.claim: Resource-based policies move management of covered resources to Microsoft 365 and replace their Power Platform allocations and linked billing plans.
claims.quote: For resources covered by the spending policy, Copilot Credit management moves to the Microsoft 365 admin center, replacing their Power Platform admin center capacity allocations and linked billing plans.

claims.where: Cost and licensing; controls[5].note; Governance guidance: Before rollout
claims.claim: These policies do not cover AI Builder credits, and Microsoft warns against moving resources using AI Builder to them.
claims.quote: Resource-based policies created in the Microsoft 365 admin center don't apply to AI Builder features or the credits they consume.

claims.claim: Microsoft 365 spending controls take precedence over Power Platform controls for covered usage.
claims.quote: If a spending policy in the Microsoft 365 admin center covers the environment or agent, its controls take precedence over the Power Platform admin center controls for that usage.

claims.claim: Existing Power Platform spending configuration remains effective until an administrator creates a resource-based policy.
claims.quote: To opt in, create a Microsoft 365 admin center resource-based spending policy. Until then, your existing Power Platform admin center configuration remains in effect.

claims.claim: The cited pages do not explain how shared autonomous agents' per-user credit totals appear in reports.

claims.claim: Learn describes the agent sharing rules in terms of Editor and Viewer permissions, including security-group and viewer-number restrictions.

claims.quote:
Use the search box to find the connector you want.

claims.claim: New-DlpPolicy -NewPolicy $NewPolicy is the automation equivalent for blocking event triggers through the Microsoft Copilot Studio connector.
claims.quote:
Creates a new DLP policy in the tenant by using the NewPolicy DLPPolicyDefinition object.
Creates a new policy with the $NewPolicy object.
claims.fix: Set controls[2].api to null and remove the corresponding table call. Retain the note that the cited New-DlpPolicy reference documents creating a policy, not assigning the Microsoft Copilot Studio connector to Blocked. A policy-creation call is not a documented equivalent for this row's connector-blocking operation.

claims.claim: The cited New-DlpPolicy reference does not describe assigning this connector to Blocked.
claims.quote: Searched the complete New-DlpPolicy reference for connector assignment and Blocked; read its syntax, example and parameters. It documents NewPolicy creation and a default connector classification, but no assignment of Microsoft Copilot Studio to Blocked.

claims.claim: The maker credential policy is immediate and applies to all agents in the environment.

claims.claim: Microsoft warns that blocking maker credentials causes scheduled or autonomous background agents to fail for missing live credentials.
claims.quote: As a result, agents triggered by scheduled or autonomous events, or that attempt to run in the background, fail due to missing credentials. All agent triggers must involve an active user.

claims.claim: An action using end-user credentials cannot perform an operation the user lacks permission to perform.
claims.quote: The action runs under the end-user's identity. If the user lacks permission for something, the agent is unable to do it on their behalf - by design.

claims.claim: The cited cost-management article recommends the AI Administrator role for spending-policy management.
